prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Lebanon's prime minister condemned the firing of rockets into northern Israel after an attack wounded two Israelis on Thursday.  He said his government is trying to determine who was responsible. U.N. soldiers on Thursday inspect the site in Lebanon thought to be the source of rockets fired into Israel. Israel's military warned Israeli civilians to stick close to shelters after police said at least four rockets hit near the city of Nahariya, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of the Lebanese border. The Israeli military said it returned fire across the border with mortars. Schools and kindergartens were closed in Nahariya and the nearby town of Shlomi, the Israel Defense Forces reported. "What happened in the south [of Lebanon] is a violation of Resolution 1701 and is rejected by Lebanon," Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora said, referring to the U.N. resolution that ended the 2006 conflict between Israel and Lebanon's Hezbollah militia. In a statement issued by his office, Siniora said he has asked Lebanese authorities to investigate the attack alongside troops from the U.N. peacekeeping force deployed along the border. He also condemned the Israeli retaliatory strikes, which the Lebanese military said inflicted no casualties.  Watch CNN's Christiane Amanpour discuss rocket attack » . There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, which came as Israeli airstrikes on Gaza, to the south, entered a 13th day. The Israeli campaign in Gaza is aimed at halting rocket fire from the Hamas-ruled Palestinian territory. Israel fought a similar battle against the Lebanese Shiite Muslim militia Hezbollah in 2006, during which Hezbollah rained rockets on cities in Israeli's north for a month before a cease-fire was reached. But Hezbollah has kept a tight rein on its forces in southern Lebanon since the cease-fire, and a number of Palestinian factions operate in southern Lebanon as well. Andrea Tenenti, a spokesman for UNIFIL, the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Lebanon, said the rockets appear to have been fired from a point about 4.5 miles east of Naqoura, where the peacekeepers are headquartered. "We've been intensifying our patrols on the ground in order to prevent any further incident," Tenenti said. He said UNIFIL's commander, Maj. Gen. Claudio Graziano, is in "constant and close contact" with both sides "and has urged maximum restraint in order to prevent any escalation of the situation." CNN's Michal Zippori in Jerusalem and Cal Perry and Nada Husseini in Beirut contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) —** Lebanon’s prime minister condemned the firing of rockets into northern Israel on Thursday after an attack wounded two Israelis, saying his government was working to determine who was responsible.

U.N. soldiers inspected a site in Lebanon believed to have been the launch point for the rockets fired into Israel.

The Israeli military warned civilians to remain close to shelters after police reported that at least four rockets had struck near Nahariya, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of the Lebanese border. The military said it responded with mortar fire across the border.

Schools and kindergartens were closed in Nahariya and the nearby town of Shlomi, according to the Israel Defense Forces.

“What happened in the south [of Lebanon] is a violation of Resolution 1701 and is rejected by Lebanon,” Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora said, referring to the U.N. resolution that ended the 2006 conflict between Israel and Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia.

In a statement issued by his office, Siniora said he had asked Lebanese authorities to investigate the attack in coordination with troops from the U.N. peacekeeping force deployed along the border. He also condemned Israel’s retaliatory strikes, which the Lebanese military said caused no casualties.

Watch CNN’s Christiane Amanpour discuss the rocket attack.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks, which occurred as Israeli airstrikes on Gaza, to the south, entered their 13th day. Israel’s campaign in Gaza is aimed at halting rocket fire from the Hamas-ruled Palestinian territory.

Israel fought a similar battle against the Lebanese Shiite Muslim militia Hezbollah in 2006. During that conflict, Hezbollah rained rockets on cities in northern Israel for a month before a ceasefire was reached.

However, Hezbollah has kept tight control over its forces in southern Lebanon since the ceasefire. A number of Palestinian factions also operate in the area.

Andrea Tenenti, a spokesman for UNIFIL, the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Lebanon, said the rockets appeared to have been fired from a point about 4.5 miles east of Naqoura, where the peacekeepers are headquartered.

“We’ve been intensifying our patrols on the ground in order to prevent any further incident,” Tenenti said.

He added that UNIFIL commander Maj. Gen. Claudio Graziano was in “constant and close contact” with both sides and “has urged maximum restraint in order to prevent any escalation of the situation.”

CNN’s Michal Zippori in Jerusalem and Cal Perry and Nada Husseini in Beirut contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) —** Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora denounced Thursday’s rocket fire into northern Israel, which injured two Israelis, and said authorities were working to identify those responsible.

U.N. peacekeepers inspected an area in Lebanon believed to be the launch site. Israeli police reported that at least four rockets landed near Nahariya, approximately 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of the Lebanese border. Israel’s military advised residents to remain near shelters and said it responded by firing mortar rounds across the frontier.

The Israel Defense Forces said schools and kindergartens were shut in Nahariya and the neighboring town of Shlomi.

Siniora described the incident in southern Lebanon as a breach of U.N. Resolution 1701, which brought an end to the 2006 war between Israel and Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia, and said Lebanon rejected the attack.

According to a statement from his office, Siniora instructed Lebanese authorities to investigate in coordination with U.N. peacekeeping troops stationed along the border. He also criticized Israel’s retaliatory fire, which caused no casualties, according to the Lebanese military.

CNN’s Christiane Amanpour discussed the rocket attack.

No group immediately took responsibility. The rockets were launched as Israel’s air campaign in Gaza, located to the south, reached its 13th day. Israel said the operation was intended to stop rockets being fired from the Hamas-controlled Palestinian territory.

In 2006, Israel fought a comparable conflict with Hezbollah, a Lebanese Shiite Muslim militia. Hezbollah fired rockets at northern Israeli cities for a month before the sides agreed to a cease-fire. Since then, Hezbollah has maintained strict control over its fighters in southern Lebanon. Several Palestinian groups also operate in that region.

Andrea Tenenti, a spokesperson for the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, said the rockets seemed to have originated roughly 4.5 miles east of Naqoura, the location of the peacekeeping mission’s headquarters.

Tenenti said UNIFIL had increased its ground patrols to help prevent another incident. He added that the force’s commander, Maj. Gen. Claudio Graziano, remained in “constant and close contact” with both parties and had called for the greatest possible restraint to avoid an escalation.

CNN’s Michal Zippori in Jerusalem, along with Cal Perry and Nada Husseini in Beirut, contributed to the report.

Siniora said the rocket launches violated U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 conflict between Israel and Hezbollah. He also condemned Israel’s military response.

Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora condemned the firing of rockets from southern Lebanon into northern Israel, saying the attack threatened Lebanon’s security and stability. Two Israelis were wounded in the incident, which prompted Israeli forces to respond with mortar fire toward the area from which the rockets were believed to have been launched.

Lebanese authorities opened an investigation in coordination with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, whose peacekeepers were deployed in the south following the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. Security forces searched for those responsible and worked to determine how the rockets had been positioned and fired.

No organization immediately claimed responsibility. Hezbollah also did not announce any involvement, raising speculation that a smaller Palestinian or militant faction may have carried out the attack. Lebanese officials stressed that the government had not authorized the launch and rejected attempts to use Lebanese territory to draw the country into another confrontation with Israel.

The exchange represented a violation of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war and called for a cessation of hostilities along the border. The resolution also expanded UNIFIL’s presence and required that southern Lebanon remain free of unauthorized armed activity.

The incident heightened fears that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza could spread to Lebanon and ignite a broader regional conflict. Lebanese and U.N. officials urged restraint, warning that even a limited exchange could escalate rapidly along the already tense Israeli-Lebanese frontier.

counterfactuals.output:
**Rockets Fired From Lebanon Into Israel Raise Fears of Wider Conflict**

**BEIRUT, Jan. 8, 2009** — Militants in southern Lebanon fired several rockets into northern Israel on Thursday, wounding at least two people and prompting Israeli artillery fire, as fighting between Israel and Hamas continued in the Gaza Strip.

The rockets struck near the Israeli city of Nahariya, according to Israeli officials. Israel responded by firing artillery shells toward the suspected launch area in southern Lebanon. No major casualties were reported there.

Lebanese Prime Minister Fouad Siniora condemned the attack and said Lebanon remained committed to U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. The Lebanese Army increased patrols in the south and worked with the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, to locate the launch site and prevent further attacks.

UNIFIL said its peacekeepers, in coordination with Lebanese troops, opened an investigation and examined the area from which the rockets were believed to have been launched. The mission described the attack as a serious violation of Resolution 1701 and urged all sides to exercise restraint.

Hezbollah denied involvement, and no group immediately made a credible claim of responsibility. Lebanese officials suggested the rockets may have been fired by a small Palestinian or other militant faction seeking to open a second front while Israel was conducting its military campaign in Gaza.

The incident heightened concern that the Gaza conflict could spread into Lebanon and revive large-scale fighting along the Israeli-Lebanese border. Israeli and Lebanese authorities, as well as U.N. officials, emphasized efforts to contain the exchange and avoid an escalation similar to the 2006 war.
